chapter_title: Concerning the Catechumen who found fault with the Elect: why he is angry.
chapter_note: Chapter is dominated by dialogue frame and pastoral exhortation about honoring the elect; core material appears mainly where a cosmological mechanism is invoked (foreign body, Flesh of Sin, mystery of the two essences, Cross of Light). The dialogue attributions (‘apostle’, ‘enlightener’) and the moral instruction are later framing/communal pedagogy rather than the oldest systematic teaching layer.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Hagiographic narrative setup (‘Once again…’, catechumen before ‘my master, the apostle’) is compilation frame language.
A catechumen’s complaint and moral evaluation of the ‘righteous’ is part of the constructed dialogue scenario; no systematic cosmological exposition, functions as a rhetorical prompt in the frame.
Dialogue attribution (‘Then our enlightener speaks…’) is a classic frame marker.

Extended ethical parable/exhortation (tree, smoke/ash, cultivate) aimed at correcting speech and attitude; lacks the impersonal cosmological mapping typical of the oldest layer and serves catechetical persuasion within the dialogue.

paragraphs.core_text: This is also the case with the elect. They are gods as they stand firm in the image of the gods. The divinity that is planted in them came to them from the heights and [dw]elt in them.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed concluding clause: ‘They have done the will of the greatness.’ This reads as a hortatory/piety summary rather than the underlying cosmological description of implanted divinity from the heights.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Contains older cosmological teaching motifs (divinity from the heights implanted/dwelling; elect as image-bearers). Ends with a devotional/commendatory line that looks like later catechetical moralizing.

paragraphs.core_text: Further, when they will be troubled and angry and resentful, [they] curse each other. However, do not you be troubled in your heart. You know, once and for all, they are established in a body that is not their own, hating the Flesh of Sin that makes the other dwell in a foreign land. Due to this they shall be angry, and say and utter hard words to each others' faces.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Process/mechanism explanation for affect (anger) grounded in cosmology/anthropology (‘body that is not their own’, personified Flesh of Sin, foreign land). Less institutional, more explanatory.

paragraphs.core_text: For you have known the mystery of the two essences, you have understood that what is good and what is evil dwell in every person. You have also understood that the saints bear a great burden on their shoulders. For you yourself have understood that they carry a great burden, they are established in the body that is not their own.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the surrounding imperatives and community-discipline prohibitions (‘do not…criticise…do not…reject…do not…distance…do not ask why…’; ‘not constructive to utter words…about the saint’) as pastoral enforcement; retained the cosmological/anthropological rationale (two essences; mixed good/evil; foreign body; burden).
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core concepts (‘mystery of the two essences’, good/evil co-dwelling; foreign body) embedded in a strongly prescriptive admonition typical of community catechesis.

paragraphs.core_text: Your hands are always free to beat the Cross of Light.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the surrounding moral invective and institutional reassurance (‘You stand in sin…eating…lusting…’; ‘the saints watch you…neither mock…be your teacher…accept you…teaching you…charities…congregation…journey…’) as late pastoral/communal discipline; retained the cosmological term ‘Cross of Light’ as a core technical entity embedded in the admonition.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Mostly pastoral policing of catechumen behavior and elect–hearer relations; only a small embedded piece of technical cosmological vocabulary (‘Cross of Light’) likely reflects older teaching terminology.
Pure exhortation to honor/love elect; no cosmological mechanism; reads as community discipline.
Narrative transition/response with ‘apostle’ attribution and emotional persuasion (‘weeping’)—frame closure device.

paragraphs.core_text: For when quarrelling will arise among the saints [ ... ] because the old man too dwells in their body; and due to this they shall take offence [ ... and] they {dispute} with one another.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed penitential address and deference formula (‘Forgive me my sins…my master…you have taught me…’) as dialogue-frame/pastoral performance; retained the anthropological mechanism (‘old man…dwells in their body’) explaining conflict.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core anthropological explanation (the ‘old man’ indwelling in the body) embedded in a staged penitential response typical of the dialogue frame.
